edges.description: The germline variant is the first hit. The genetics series predicts that every tumour also needs a second, somatic DICER1 hit, and proposes that it takes place in the embryonic pituitary. A 2014 case report concludes from its one tumour that loss of function of both DICER1 alleles appears crucial to start the tumour.
In these tumours the RNase IIIb hotspot mutations cause improper processing of microRNA precursors, with aberrant 5p-derived products and mature microRNAs skewed from 5p towards 3p.

How the microRNA imbalance produces the embryonic-appearing tumour is not established; the genetics series leaves the mechanism to be explored, and the molecular study names the pathways that are dysregulated (RAR, WNT and NOTCH) and finds the PI3K pathway activated.

nodes.description: Given after surgery to five of the 17 children of the outcome series (six had adjuvant therapy of any kind); adjuvant therapy as a whole was not significantly associated with survival in the series. Regimens varied from child to child: temozolomide in two children, after subtotal resection in one, whose tumour progressed locally 20 months from diagnosis, and after a biopsy and again after a near-total resection in the other; a Pediatric Oncology Group protocol the outcome series' Table 1 calls 'baby POG' and the Australian and New Zealand Children's Cancer Study Group baby brain protocol without autologous stem cell transplant; and cyclophosphamide, vincristine, methotrexate, carboplatin and etoposide in a child who died of a catheter-related complication after four months of follow-up. In one child, recurrent hypercortisolism improved after chemotherapy. From MGMT immunolabelling of 40-60%, the 2012 report suggested an incomplete response to temozolomide, a prediction from the staining rather than an observed response. A 19-year-old woman whose pathology suggested a pituitary blastoma had chemotherapy and radiotherapy after subtotal resection.

nodes.description: A heterozygous germline DICER1 variant, most often one predicted to inactivate the allele, is found in most children tested: 9 of 10 in the genetics series, 12 of 13 in the outcome series and 11 of 14 in a 2022 review. In the genetics series it was known to be inherited in five children and de novo in two. On its own it is thought not to produce the tumour: the genetics series predicts a second, somatic hit in every case. In the outcome series it was inherited in 6 of the 8 children whose families were tested, and relatives in 5 of those 6 families had DICER1-related conditions. In a 2014 case report the germline frameshift allele made up 12% of the DICER1 transcripts in the child's leukocytes and none of those in the tumour.

nodes.description: The transforming event: a somatic hit on the remaining DICER1 allele in the tumour, usually a missense mutation at a metal ion-binding residue of the RNase IIIb domain, and in a minority loss of the wild-type allele. In the genetics series eight of the nine tumour changes found were confirmed to be somatic; seven of the nine were predicted to hit the RNase IIIb catalytic site and the other two were losses of the wild-type allele. In one of those two children (case 12 of the genetics series) the authors infer that the loss, together with the germline variant, would leave no normal DICER1 in the affected cells. The genetics series concludes that a somatic RNase IIIb mutation appears to be a critical second hit. In the outcome series, whose cohort overlaps the genetics series, 13 of 14 tumours tested had a DICER1 change: a hotspot mutation in 11 and loss of heterozygosity in 2. A 2014 case report, whose child is case 14 of the outcome series, found the child's germline frameshift variant and a somatic E1813V missense change together in one tumour. Whole-genome sequencing of tumours in a 2021 molecular study found very few somatic alterations, suggesting that few other changes accompany the DICER1 hits.

nodes.description: The first treatment in every child of the outcome series, in four of them in stages: gross or near-total resection in 7, subtotal resection in 9 and biopsy alone in 1. The extent of resection was the one treatment factor associated with survival, and surgery was the only treatment in five of the nine survivors: of the seven children treated by surgery alone who lived beyond six weeks, five became long-term survivors, four after gross total and one after subtotal resection. The series' authors judge that complete or near-complete resection may be enough for disease control in some patients, while noting that the small numbers limit robust analysis of prognostic factors. The 2012 report's abstract describes its three additional cases (one previously published as a pituitary adenoma; by the genetics series' Table 1, two of them are its cases 3 and 5, which match the outcome series' cases 3 and 5 by case number, sex and age) as subtotally resected; in two adult case reports a tumour in a 19-year-old woman whose pathology suggested a pituitary blastoma was subtotally removed, and a 27-year-old man had surgical decompression.
